References

On this page

Hill tensors by transformation: closed forms derived step by step ​

The whole page as one script

Every block of this page, in order, is scripts/98_hill_transformation_2020.jl. From a clone of the repository, julia --project=docs -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' once, then julia scripts/98_hill_transformation_2020.jl, runs it end to end.

Before this page

The section Reduction to a sphere and the section Transversely isotropic matrix coaxial with a spheroid of the theory page on Hill tensors, which state the results this page derives, and the tutorial Hill tensors by reduction to a sphere, which drives the reduction through the library.

Barthélémy (2020) shows that the Hill polarization tensor of any ellipsoid is that of a sphere in a transformed medium, and draws two closed forms from it: an ellipsoid in an elliptically orthotropic matrix, and a spheroid in a coaxial transversely isotropic matrix, with the flat and needle limits of the latter. This page goes through the paper in its order, with the equation numbers of the article, and checks every step in one of three ways:

  • by computation, against the definition of the Hill tensor integrated on the unit sphere and against the numerical back-ends of the package;

  • by symbolic computation, with SymPy, for the identities the derivation rests on: they hold for free symbols, not for a sample of values;

  • by a transcription in Julia of the Python script appended to the paper, whose Figure 1 is drawn again here, against the closed form the package evaluates.

Everything is written in the tensor algebra of TensND: ⊗ and ⊠ˢ for the tensor products, ⋅ and ⊡ for the simple and double contractions, ⊙ for the full contraction of two fourth-order tensors, inv of a tensor. No component is read by index except to draw the figure.

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization
using TensND
using LinearAlgebra
using Printf
using QuadGK: gauss
using ForwardDiff
using SymPyPythonCall
using Plots
gr()
default(; left_margin = 5Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 5Plots.mm)

relgap(P, Q) = norm(P - Q) / norm(Q)

1. The transformation (Section 2 of the paper) ​

The Hill tensor as an integral over the unit sphere ​

The paper starts from the expression of the Hill tensor of the ellipsoid      in a matrix as an integral over the unit sphere (eq. 1):

where is any invertible tensor, symmetric or not. The product    symmetrizes over the first two and the last two indices. TensND's ⊠ˢ symmetrizes over the last two only, so that the four terms are the half sum of    and   :

julia
sandwich(a, N) = ((a ⊗ a) ⊠ˢ N + N ⊠ˢ (a ⊗ a)) / 2
hill_integrand(y, C) = sandwich(y, inv(y ⋅ C ⋅ y))

The integrand is a smooth function on the sphere. A Gauss-Legendre rule in   and the trapezoidal rule in the longitude , exact for the trigonometric polynomials the odd powers of come with, converge exponentially; f receives the unit vector and returns the tensor to average:

julia
function sphere_average(f; nz = 96, nφ = 192)
    zs, ws = gauss(nz)
    return sum(
        w * f(TensND.Tens([sqrt(1 - z^2) * cos(φ), sqrt(1 - z^2) * sin(φ), z]))
            for (z, w) in zip(zs, ws) for φ in range(0, 2π; length = nφ + 1)[1:(end - 1)]
    ) * (2π / nφ) / (4π)
end

hill_by_definition(A, C) = (Ainv = inv(A); sphere_average(ζ -> hill_integrand(Ainv ⋅ ζ, C)))

The matrix and the shape of this section are deliberately generic: a triclinic stiffness, and a non-symmetric , a rotation times a symmetric tensor of semi-axes . As   , the ellipsoid is that of , which the package builds from its semi-axes and principal directions:

julia
C_tri = TensND.from_mandel(
    [
        210.0 80.0 75.0 5.0 4.0 3.0;
        80.0 195.0 90.0 -2.0 3.0 -1.0;
        75.0 90.0 220.0 1.0 -2.0 2.0;
        5.0 -2.0 1.0 60.0 2.5 1.5;
        4.0 3.0 -2.0 2.5 65.0 -1.0;
        3.0 -1.0 2.0 1.5 -1.0 55.0
    ], CanonicalBasis{3, Float64}()
)
R = Matrix(rot3(0.3, 0.8, -0.5))
S = TensND.Tens(Symmetric(R * Diagonal([2.0, 1.0, 0.5]) * transpose(R)))
Q = TensND.Tens(Matrix(rot3(1.1, -0.4, 0.7)))
A = Q ⋅ S

"Ellipsoid of `A`: semi-axes and axes from the eigenpairs of `Aᵀ⋅A`."
function ellipsoid_of(A)
    F = eigen(Symmetric(Array(components_canon(transpose(A) ⋅ A))))
    V = F.vectors * Diagonal([1, 1, sign(det(F.vectors))])      # a rotation
    return Ellipsoid(sqrt.(F.values)..., V)
end

P_ref = hill_tensor(ellipsoid_of(A), C_tri; method = :residues, abstol = 1.0e-13, reltol = 1.0e-12)
@printf "eq. 1 on the unit sphere against the residues:   %.1e\n" relgap(hill_by_definition(A, C_tri), P_ref)
eq. 1 on the unit sphere against the residues:   4.1e-15

The rotation only rotates the integration variable, so it leaves the Hill tensor unchanged, as the definition says:

julia
@printf "P(Q⋅S, C) against P(S, C):                       %.1e\n" relgap(hill_by_definition(A, C_tri), hill_by_definition(S, C_tri))
P(Q⋅S, C) against P(S, C):                       3.2e-13

The change of variable     gives the other classical form (eq. 9), in which the shape appears through a denominator:

julia
hill_by_xi(A, C) = det(A) * sphere_average(ξ -> hill_integrand(ξ, C) / norm(A ⋅ ξ)^3; nz = 160, nφ = 320)
@printf "eq. 9 against the residues:                      %.1e\n" relgap(hill_by_xi(S, C_tri), P_ref)
eq. 9 against the residues:                      9.3e-15

The denominator   varies by a factor 64 over the sphere for these semi-axes, and the same rule needs more points for the same accuracy: this is the difficulty the transformation removes.

Moving the shape onto the stiffness ​

In eq. 1 the shape enters through   only. Writing   , the acoustic tensor and the sandwich product become         and         (eq. 3). Any two pairs and that give the same    (eq. 4) therefore have Hill tensors related by (eq. 7)

The transposition is the major one,  , and is a stiffness whenever is one. The relation holds for any invertible ; here a second rotated triaxial shape:

julia
function hill_by_transformation(A, C, Ã, hill_of)
    M = (inv(A) ⋅ Ã) ⊠ˢ (inv(A) ⋅ Ã)
    Mᵀ = TensND.Tensors.majortranspose(M)
    return M ⊡ hill_of(Ã, Mᵀ ⊡ C ⊡ M) ⊡ Mᵀ
end

Ã = TensND.Tens(Matrix(rot3(-0.2, 1.3, 0.4))) ⋅
    TensND.Tens(Diagonal([1.0, 3.0, 1.5]))
@printf "eq. 7 with an arbitrary Ã against the residues:  %.1e\n" relgap(hill_by_transformation(A, C_tri, Ã, hill_by_definition), P_ref)
eq. 7 with an arbitrary Ã against the residues:  3.1e-14

With   the transformed shape is the unit sphere (eq. 8), the reduction to a sphere: every Hill tensor is that of a sphere in the medium    . A numerical method may treat the sphere only, where   ; here the residue algorithm of the package takes the sphere:

julia
sphere_by_residues(_, C̃) = hill_tensor(Ellipsoid(1.0), C̃; method = :residues, abstol = 1.0e-13, reltol = 1.0e-12)
P_sph = hill_by_transformation(A, C_tri, TensISO{3}(1.0), sphere_by_residues)
@printf "eq. 8, the sphere by residues:                   %.1e\n" relgap(P_sph, P_ref)
eq. 8, the sphere by residues:                   2.3e-15

2. An ellipsoid in an elliptically orthotropic matrix (Section 3) ​

The elliptically orthotropic matrix (eq. 10)       , with symmetric positive definite, is isotropic for  . The algebra of the tensor products carries it through the stretch (eq. 11):

Take with principal directions of its own, unrelated to those of the ellipsoid:

julia
λ, μ = 2.0, 1.5
RD = Matrix(rot3(0.7, 0.5, 1.9))
D = TensND.Tens(Symmetric(RD * Diagonal([1.6, 1.0, 0.7]) * transpose(RD)))
C_eo = λ * (D ⊗ D) + 2μ * (D ⊠ˢ D)

B = inv(A) ⊠ˢ inv(A)
Bᵀ = TensND.Tensors.majortranspose(B)
D′ = transpose(inv(A)) ⋅ D ⋅ inv(A)
@printf "eq. 11:  %.1e\n" relgap(Bᵀ ⊡ C_eo ⊡ B, λ * (D′ ⊗ D′) + 2μ * (D′ ⊠ˢ D′))
eq. 11:  9.4e-17

With the square roots taken on the principal directions of and    (eq. 12),   : eq. 4 holds with the isotropic        (eq. 13), and eq. 7 gives (eq. 14)

The isotropic Hill tensor of the ellipsoid has a closed form in elliptic integrals, which the package evaluates: the Hill tensor of an arbitrary ellipsoid in an elliptically orthotropic matrix is a closed form too.

julia
D_mh = TensND.Tens(Symmetric(inv(sqrt(Symmetric(Array(components_canon(D)))))))
Ã_eo = A ⋅ D_mh
@printf "D′ = Ã⁻ᵀ⋅Ã⁻¹:  %.1e\n" relgap(D′, transpose(inv(Ã_eo)) ⋅ inv(Ã_eo))

C_iso = TensISO{3}(3λ + 2μ, 2μ)              # λ 𝟏⊗𝟏 + 2μ 𝟏⊠ˢ𝟏
B_D = D_mh ⊠ˢ D_mh
P_eo = B_D ⊡ hill_tensor(ellipsoid_of(Ã_eo), C_iso) ⊡ B_D
P_eo_num = hill_tensor(ellipsoid_of(A), C_eo; method = :residues, abstol = 1.0e-13, reltol = 1.0e-12)
@printf "eq. 14 against the residues:  %.1e\n" relgap(P_eo, P_eo_num)
D′ = Ã⁻ᵀ⋅Ã⁻¹:  1.4e-15
eq. 14 against the residues:  3.1e-15

Conversely, eq. 5 maps an isotropic onto elliptically orthotropic matrices only: the method reaches no other symmetry from the isotropic case, as Pouya (2000), Pouya and Zaoui (2006) had observed.

3. A spheroid in a coaxial transversely isotropic matrix (Section 4) ​

The spheroid has the axis and the aspect ratio  ; since the Hill tensor ignores a homothety of the shape, ``\boldsymbol{A} = \underline{e}_1\otimes\underline{e}_1 + \underline{e}_2\otimes\underline{e}_2

  • \omega,\underline{e}_3\otimes\underline{e}_3`` (eq. 16). The matrix is

transversely isotropic about the same axis, with the five constants , and its Walpole decomposition (eq. 17) is the one TensND stores (Walpole basis):

The derivation is carried out on free symbols. The Walpole tensors are orthogonal for , of squared norms , which gives the coefficients of any transversely isotropic tensor without reading a component:

julia
e₃ = (Sym(0), Sym(0), Sym(1))
W₁, W₂, W₃, W₄, W₅, W₆ = walpole_basis(e₃)
walpole(X) = (W₁ ⊙ X, W₂ ⊙ X, (W₃ + W₄) ⊙ X / 2, W₅ ⊙ X / 2, W₆ ⊙ X / 2)
(W₁ ⊙ W₁, W₂ ⊙ W₂, W₃ ⊙ W₃, W₄ ⊙ W₄, W₅ ⊙ W₅, W₆ ⊙ W₆, W₃ ⊙ W₄, W₁ ⊙ W₂)
(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 0, 0)

The transformed medium (eqs. 18–20) ​

The stretch of the spheroid is diagonal, and     divides each component by to the number of indices equal to 3 (eq. 18). In the Walpole basis (eq. 19):

julia
ω = symbols("omega", positive = true)
C₁₁, C₁₂, C₁₃, C₃₃, C₄₄ = symbols("C_1111 C_1122 C_1133 C_3333 C_2323", positive = true)
C_TI = tens_ti(C₁₁, C₁₂, C₁₃, C₃₃, C₄₄, e₃)
A_sph = TensND.Tens(Diagonal(Sym[1, 1, ω]))
B_sph = inv(A_sph) ⊠ˢ inv(A_sph)
ℓ̃ = walpole(B_sph ⊡ C_TI ⊡ B_sph)
ℓ̃ .- (C₃₃ / ω^4, C₁₁ + C₁₂, sqrt(Sym(2)) * C₁₃ / ω^2, C₁₁ - C₁₂, 2 * C₄₄ / ω^2) .|> simplify
(0, 0, 0, 0, 0)

is thus transversely isotropic about , of constants  ,  ,  ,  ,  . So is the Hill tensor   of the sphere, and carried back by eq. 8 the Hill tensor of the spheroid has the Walpole coefficients of divided by the same powers of (eq. 20):

julia
p̃ = symbols("pt_1 pt_2 pt_3 pt_5 pt_6")
P̃_sym = TensND.TensTI{4}(p̃..., e₃)
walpole(B_sph ⊡ P̃_sym ⊡ B_sph) .- (p̃[1] / ω^4, p̃[2], p̃[3] / ω^2, p̃[4], p̃[5] / ω^2) .|> simplify
(0, 0, 0, 0, 0)

The sphere in the transformed medium (eqs. 21–29) ​

On the sphere,  . In the spherical coordinates of colatitude and longitude , with   (eqs. 21–22),

The integral over the longitude. Both the medium and the direction field are invariant by the rotations about : the integrand at is the integrand at   rotated by . Its average over is transversely isotropic, and its full contraction with each Walpole tensor, invariant by those rotations, is that of the integrand at  . The integral over is therefore the projection of times the integrand at   on the Walpole basis (eq. 23), and the factor leaves a half:

julia
z = symbols("z", real = true)
c̃₁₁, c̃₁₂, c̃₁₃, c̃₃₃, c̃₄₄ = (C₁₁, C₁₂, C₁₃ / ω^2, C₃₃ / ω^4, C₄₄ / ω^2)
C̃ = tens_ti(c̃₁₁, c̃₁₂, c̃₁₃, c̃₃₃, c̃₄₄, e₃)
ζ₀ = TensND.Tens(Sym[sqrt(1 - z^2), 0, z])
Ñ = inv(ζ₀ ⋅ C̃ ⋅ ζ₀)
p̃ᶻ = walpole(sandwich(ζ₀, Ñ)) ./ 2

The same average computed numerically, at a few values of , with the trapezoidal rule in on numerical moduli:

julia
let vals = Dict(ω => 0.3, C₁₁ => 2.179, C₁₂ => 0.579, C₁₃ => 0.689, C₃₃ => 10.345, C₄₄ => 1.0)
    C̃_num = tens_ti((N(subs(c, vals...)) for c in (c̃₁₁, c̃₁₂, c̃₁₃, c̃₃₃, c̃₄₄))..., (0.0, 0.0, 1.0))
    W_num = walpole_basis((0.0, 0.0, 1.0))
    gaps = map((-0.9, -0.2, 0.4, 0.7)) do zv
        ring = sum(
            hill_integrand(TensND.Tens([sqrt(1 - zv^2) * cos(φ), sqrt(1 - zv^2) * sin(φ), zv]), C̃_num)
                for φ in range(0, 2π; length = 65)[1:(end - 1)]
        ) / 64 / 2
        sym = [N(subs(p, z => zv, vals...)) for p in p̃ᶻ]
        num = (W_num[1] ⊙ ring, W_num[2] ⊙ ring, (W_num[3] + W_num[4]) ⊙ ring / 2, W_num[5] ⊙ ring / 2, W_num[6] ⊙ ring / 2)
        maximum(abs.(sym .- num))
    end
    @printf "projection at φ = 0 against the average over φ:  %.1e\n" maximum(gaps)
end
projection at φ = 0 against the average over φ:  5.6e-17

The integral over the colatitude. Substituting eq. 25 into eq. 24, each is an even polynomial in over , plus, for and , one over . Integrated over  , the monomials and give the integrals

divided by and by respectively. The map below performs that integration on a rational function of the form  : it reads off and as the residues of the partial-fraction decomposition in the symbols and , which stand for the two denominators:

julia
𝒥 = symbols("J_0 J_2 J_4 J_6")
ℐ = symbols("I_0 I_2 I_4")
Qs, Rs = symbols("Q R", positive = true)

"Integral over ``[-1, 1]`` of `u(z)/q(z) + v(z)/r(z)`, written in the 𝒥ₖ and ℐₖ."
function integrate_z(expr)
    e = expand(subs(expr, q => Qs, r => Rs))
    u, v = expand(e.coeff(1 / Qs)), expand(e.coeff(1 / Rs))
    iszero(simplify(e - u / Qs - v / Rs)) || error("not of the form u/q + v/r")
    Ju = sum(u.coeff(z, 2k) * 𝒥[k + 1] for k in 0:3) / a
    Iv = sum(v.coeff(z, 2k) * ℐ[k + 1] for k in 0:2) / c̃₄₄
    return simplify(Ju + Iv)
end

Substituted in eq. 24 the components of eq. 25 give, once integrated, the Walpole coefficients of (eq. 29):

    z^2 * eq25[2] / 2,

    z * s * eq25[3] / (2 * sqrt(Sym(2))),
    ((1 - z^2) * eq25[1] + (1 - z^2) * eq25[4]) / 8,
    (z^2 * eq25[1] + z^2 * eq25[4] + (1 - z^2) * eq25[2] + 2 * z * s * eq25[3]) / 8,
)

    ((c̃₁₁ + c̃₃₃ + 2c̃₁₃) * J₄ - 2 * (c̃₁₁ + c̃₁₃) * J₂ + c̃₁₁ * J₀) / (8 * c̃₄₄ * c̃₃₃) + I₂ / (8 * c̃₄₄),

Back to the spheroid (eqs. 30–36) ​

The roots of eq. 27, written with , are times the roots of the same polynomial written with (eq. 30): substituting   divides it by . Likewise   (eq. 33):

(
    simplify(poly(ω^2 * Y, c̃₁₁, c̃₁₃, c̃₃₃, c̃₄₄) - poly(Y, C₁₁, C₁₃, C₃₃, C₄₄) / ω^2),

The roots are eq. 31, with the discriminant of eq. 32:

julia

The integrals (Appendix D) ​

Single root. With        , the integral of is an inverse hyperbolic tangent. For a real   (the integrand is then positive and regular), its derivative checks the primitive, and its value at    is that of Table D.1, by the identity  :

julia

I₀_tab = 2 * acosh(η) / (η * sqrt(k²))
(
    simplify(diff(F₀, z) - 1 / (η^2 - k² * z^2)),
    simplify(diff(atanh(sqrt(k²) / η) - acosh(η), η)),
    subs(atanh(sqrt(k²) / η) - acosh(η), η => 1),
)
(0, 0, 0)

and follow from without a new integral:    , so that      . The recurrence reproduces the second and third columns of Table D.1:

julia

I₄_tab = Sym(2) / 3 * (3 * η^3 * acosh(η) + (1 - 4η^2) * sqrt(k²)) / k²^(Sym(5) / 2)
(
    simplify(z^2 / (η^2 - k² * z^2) - (1 - η^2 / (η^2 - k² * z^2)) / (1 - η^2)),
    simplify(I₂_rec - I₂_tab),
    simplify(I₄_rec - I₄_tab),
)
(0, 0, 0)

julia

4. The script of the paper, in Julia ​

The Python script appended to the paper evaluates the integrals of Tables D.1 and D.2 in complex arithmetic and the coefficients of eq. 36. Its transcription below accepts any number type: the moduli and the aspect ratio are promoted together, the arithmetic runs in complex numbers of that type, and the imaginary parts, which cancel, are dropped at the end. The square root and the inverse hyperbolic cosine of Julia have the principal branches the paper specifies (Appendix D), those of Python's cmath. The script switches to the special rows of the tables within of them; here they are taken on exact equality only, which is the point the formulas of the general rows cannot be evaluated at.

julia
"Integrals ``(\\mathcal{I}_0, \\mathcal{I}_2, \\mathcal{I}_4)(\\eta)`` of Table D.1."
function 𝓘(η)
    k² = η^2 - 1
    iszero(k²) && return (2, 2 // 3, 2 // 5) .* one(η)
    sk, ac = sqrt(k²), acosh(η)
    return (2ac / (η * sk), 2 * (η * ac - sk) / (k² * sk), 2 * (3η^3 * ac + (1 - 4η^2) * sk) / (3 * k²^2 * sk))
end

"Integrals ``(\\mathcal{J}_0, \\mathcal{J}_2, \\mathcal{J}_4)(\\eta_1, \\eta_2)`` of Table D.2."
function 𝓙(η₁, η₂)
    η₁^2 == η₂^2 || return ((1 - η₁^2) .* 𝓘(η₁) .- (1 - η₂^2) .* 𝓘(η₂)) ./ (η₂^2 - η₁^2)
    k² = η₁^2 - 1
    iszero(k²) && return (2, 2 // 3, 2 // 5) .* one(η₁)
    sk, ac = sqrt(k²), acosh(η₁)
    return ((ac + η₁ * sk) / (η₁^3 * sk), (η₁ * sk - ac) / (η₁ * k² * sk), ((2 + η₁^2) * sk - 3η₁ * ac) / (k²^2 * sk))
end

"""
    hill_ti_paper(ω, C1111, C1122, C1133, C3333, C2323)

Hill tensor of a spheroid of aspect ratio `ω` coaxial with a transversely
isotropic matrix of axis ``\\underline{e}_3``, by eqs. 31–36 of the paper.
"""
function hill_ti_paper(ω, C1111, C1122, C1133, C3333, C2323)
    T = promote_type(typeof(ω), typeof(C1111), typeof(C1122), typeof(C1133), typeof(C3333), typeof(C2323))
    w, c11, c12, c13, c33, c44 = Complex{T}.((ω, C1111, C1122, C1133, C3333, C2323))
    Δ = (c11 * c33 - c13^2) * (c11 * c33 - c13^2 - 4c13 * c44 - 4c44^2)            # eq. 32
    γ₁ = sqrt((c11 * c33 - c13^2 - 2c13 * c44 + sqrt(Δ)) / (2c44 * c33))             # eq. 31
    γ₂ = sqrt((c11 * c33 - c13^2 - 2c13 * c44 - sqrt(Δ)) / (2c44 * c33))
    γ₃ = sqrt((c11 - c12) / (2c44))                                                  # eq. 33
    J₀, J₂, J₄ = 𝓙(w * γ₁, w * γ₂) ./ (c44 * c33)                                    # eq. 34
    I₀, I₂, _ = 𝓘(w * γ₃) ./ c44
    w² = w^2
    p₁ = ((c44 - w² * c11) * J₄ + w² * c11 * J₂) / 2                                 # eq. 36a
    p₂ = w² * ((w² * c44 - c33) * J₄ + (c33 - 2w² * c44) * J₂ + w² * c44 * J₀) / 4    # eq. 36b
    p₃ = w² * (c44 + c13) * (J₄ - J₂) / (2 * sqrt(T(2)))                             # eq. 36c
    p₅ = p₂ / 2 + w² * (I₀ - I₂) / 8                                                 # eq. 36d
    p₆ = ((w²^2 * c11 + c33 + 2w² * c13) * J₄ - 2w² * (w² * c11 + c13) * J₂ + w²^2 * c11 * J₀) / 8 + I₂ / 8
    return TensTI{4}(real.((p₁, p₂, p₃, p₅, p₆))..., (zero(T), zero(T), one(T)))     # eq. 35
end

The integrals against a quadrature. For two real roots, then a pair of complex conjugate ones, which a positive definite matrix may have, the transcription agrees with a Gauss-Kronrod quadrature of the definitions. The sign printed in the third row of Table D.2 gives the opposite:

julia
using QuadGK: quadgk
for (e₁, e₂) in ((1.7 + 0im, 0.6 + 0im), (1.2 + 0.5im, 1.2 - 0.5im))
    D(e, x) = x^2 + e^2 * (1 - x^2)
    quad = [quadgk(x -> x^k / (D(e₁, x) * D(e₂, x)), -1, 1; rtol = 1.0e-14)[1] for k in (0, 2, 4)]
    as_printed = ((e₁^2 - 1) .* 𝓘(e₁) .- (e₂^2 - 1) .* 𝓘(e₂)) ./ (e₂^2 - e₁^2)
    @printf "η = %s, %s:  script %.1e   Table D.2 as printed %.1e\n" e₁ e₂ maximum(abs.(collect(𝓙(e₁, e₂)) .- quad)) maximum(abs.(collect(as_printed) .- quad))
end
η = 1.7 + 0.0im, 0.6 + 0.0im:  script 3.3e-16   Table D.2 as printed 3.4e+00
η = 1.2 + 0.5im, 1.2 - 0.5im:  script 4.4e-16   Table D.2 as printed 2.2e+00

The two agree along the whole sweep, and both with nested Gauss-Kronrod quadratures of the general anisotropic formula, which share no code with either:

    @printf "ω = %5.2f   against the quadrature:  %.1e\n" ω relgap(hill_ti_paper(ω, C_sev...), P_quad)

Where the formulas as written lose digits ​

The partial fractions of Table D.2 divide by  . A matrix close to isotropy has close acoustic roots, and the general row then subtracts nearly equal terms; the exact isotropic matrix lands, after the rounding of , on it as well. Take an isotropic matrix of moduli  ,   and stiffen by a relative :

julia
for δ in (1.0e-2, 1.0e-4, 1.0e-6, 1.0e-8, 0.0)
    moduli = (3.0, 1.0, 1.0, 3.0 * (1 + δ), 1.0)
    P_pkg = hill_tensor(Ellipsoid(1.0, 1.0, 0.5), tens_ti(moduli..., (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)))
    @printf "δ = %.0e   transcription against the package:  %.1e\n" δ relgap(hill_ti_paper(0.5, moduli...), P_pkg)
end
δ = 1e-02   transcription against the package:  8.3e-16
δ = 1e-04   transcription against the package:  6.5e-15
δ = 1e-06   transcription against the package:  8.4e-14
δ = 1e-08   transcription against the package:  2.0e-12
δ = 0e+00   transcription against the package:  3.4e-16

The error grows as shrinks: the formulas are exact, their evaluation is not. The package evaluates the same integrals in three regimes that never subtract them, described in Spheroid in a transversely isotropic matrix, and stays at rounding level there, derivatives included.

5. The flat spheroid and the crack (Section 4.3) ​

The expansions of the integrals (Appendix D) ​

For   , the case of a flat spheroid, the primitive of is an inverse tangent and Table D.1 takes its real form,  :

julia
F₀_flat = atan(sqrt(1 - η^2) * z / η) / (η * sqrt(1 - η^2))
(
    simplify(diff(F₀_flat, z) - 1 / (η^2 + (1 - η^2) * z^2)),
    simplify(diff(atan(sqrt(1 - η^2) / η) - acos(η), η)),
    subs(atan(sqrt(1 - η^2) / η) - acos(η), η => 1),
)
(0, 0, 0)

The same recurrence as above gives and . Their expansions are those of a function of one variable, which SymPy takes at   once; with   they are eqs. D.2:

julia
γ, γ₁, γ₂, γ₃ = symbols("gamma gamma_1 gamma_2 gamma_3", positive = true)
I₀_flat(e) = 2 * acos(e) / (e * sqrt(1 - e^2))
I_series = let I₀s = series(I₀_flat(η), η, 0, 6).removeO()
    I₂s = series((2 - η^2 * I₀s) / (1 - η^2), η, 0, 6).removeO()
    I₄s = series((Sym(2) / 3 - η^2 * I₂s) / (1 - η^2), η, 0, 6).removeO()
    (I₀s, I₂s, I₄s)
end

The coefficient of ωᵏ in a Laurent polynomial in ω whose lowest power is ω⁻³: brought over one denominator free of ω, its numerator is a polynomial.

julia
function laurent(e, k)
    num, den = sympy.fraction(cancel(e * ω^3))
    return simplify(sympy.Poly(num, ω).coeff_monomial(ω^(k + 3)) / den)
end
I_at(γx) = [subs(Ik, η => ω * γx) for Ik in I_series]
eqD2 = (PI / (γ * ω) - 2 + PI * γ * ω / 2, 2 - PI * γ * ω, Sym(2) / 3)
[laurent(I_at(γ)[n] - eqD2[n], k) for n in 1:3, k in -1:1]

The partial fractions then give those of (eqs. D.3), with    . The division by     is exact, coefficient by coefficient in :

julia
Σ = γ₁^2 + γ₁ * γ₂ + γ₂^2
J_flat = map(I_at(γ₁), I_at(γ₂)) do I₁, I₂
    cancel(((1 - ω^2 * γ₁^2) * I₁ - (1 - ω^2 * γ₂^2) * I₂) / (ω^2 * (γ₂^2 - γ₁^2)))
end
eqD3 = (
    PI / (γ₁ * γ₂ * (γ₁ + γ₂) * ω^3) + PI / (2 * (γ₁ + γ₂) * ω) - Sym(2) / 3 + PI * Σ * ω / (8 * (γ₁ + γ₂)),
    PI / ((γ₁ + γ₂) * ω) - 2 + PI * Σ * ω / (2 * (γ₁ + γ₂)),
    2 - PI * Σ * ω / (γ₁ + γ₂),
)
[laurent(J_flat[n] - eqD3[n], k) for n in 1:3, k in -3:1]

The expansions are derived for real roots; both sides are rational in and and symmetric in them, so that they hold for a pair of complex conjugate roots as well, by analytic continuation.

The Hill tensor of a flat spheroid (eqs. 37–39) ​

Substituted into eq. 36, the expansions give the first two terms of     . The leading term (eq. 37) is      , that of a crack, and the next one has the Walpole coefficients of eq. 38:

julia
flat = Dict(J₀ => eqD3[1], J₂ => eqD3[2], J₄ => eqD3[3], I₀ => subs(eqD2[1], γ => γ₃), I₂ => subs(eqD2[2], γ => γ₃))
p_flat = [subs(p, flat...) for p in eq36]
P⁰ = [laurent(p, 0) for p in p_flat]
P¹ = [laurent(p, 1) for p in p_flat]
eq37 = walpole(sandwich(TensND.Tens(Sym[0, 0, 1]), inv(TensND.Tens(Sym[0, 0, 1]) ⋅ C_TI ⋅ TensND.Tens(Sym[0, 0, 1]))))
eq38 = (
    PI / (2 * (γ₁ + γ₂)) * (C₁₁ - Σ * C₄₄) / (C₄₄ * C₃₃),
    PI / (4 * (γ₁ + γ₂)) * (1 / (γ₁ * γ₂ * C₃₃) + 1 / C₄₄),
    -sqrt(Sym(2)) * PI / (4 * (γ₁ + γ₂)) * (C₁₃ + C₄₄) / (C₄₄ * C₃₃),
    PI / 8 * (1 / (γ₁ * γ₂ * (γ₁ + γ₂) * C₃₃) + (1 / (γ₁ + γ₂) + 1 / γ₃) / C₄₄),
    PI / 8 * ((C₁₁ - 2γ₁ * γ₂ * C₁₃ - γ₁ * γ₂ * Σ * C₃₃) / (γ₁ * γ₂ * (γ₁ + γ₂) * C₄₄ * C₃₃) - γ₃ / C₄₄),
)
(simplify.(P⁰ .- eq37), simplify.(P¹ .- eq38))
(SymPyCore.Sym{PythonCall.Py}[0, 0, 0, 0, 0], SymPyCore.Sym{PythonCall.Py}[0, 0, 0, 0, 0])

The crack compliance (eqs. 40–41) ​

The second Hill tensor      becomes singular as the spheroid flattens, and its inverse grows as . The crack compliance is the limit (eq. 40)

With     on free symbols for the five coefficients of , the inverse of a transversely isotropic tensor stays one, and the limit has the two Walpole coefficients of eq. 41, which depend on only:

julia
p¹ = symbols("p1_1 p1_2 p1_3 p1_5 p1_6")
P_lin = TensND.TensTI{4}((P⁰ .+ ω .* p¹)..., e₃)
Q_lin = C_TI - C_TI ⊡ P_lin ⊡ C_TI
H_sym = [subs(cancel(ω * h), ω => 0) for h in walpole(inv(Q_lin))]
eq41 = (
    -1 / (C₃₃^2 * p¹[1] + 2 * C₁₃^2 * p¹[2] + 2 * sqrt(Sym(2)) * C₃₃ * C₁₃ * p¹[3]),
    0, 0, 0,
    -1 / (4 * C₄₄^2 * p¹[5]),
)
simplify.(H_sym .- eq41)

On the matrix of Figure 1, the crack compliance of eq. 41, with the coefficients of eq. 38, is the limit of   computed with second_hill_tensor, and the tensor of a penny-shaped crack that the package builds from its crack opening displacement tensor,      (see cod_tensor):

julia
γ_num = let c11 = C_sev[1], c12 = C_sev[2], c13 = C_sev[3], c33 = C_sev[4], c44 = C_sev[5]
    Δn = complex((c11 * c33 - c13^2) * (c11 * c33 - c13^2 - 4c13 * c44 - 4c44^2))
    X = c11 * c33 - c13^2 - 2c13 * c44
    (sqrt((X + sqrt(Δn)) / (2c44 * c33)), sqrt((X - sqrt(Δn)) / (2c44 * c33)), sqrt(complex((c11 - c12) / (2c44))))
end

eqs. 38 and 41 as Julia functions, evaluated on the complex roots.

julia
p¹_num = [lambdify(e, (C₁₁, C₁₂, C₁₃, C₃₃, C₄₄, γ₁, γ₂, γ₃))(complex.(C_sev)..., γ_num...) for e in eq38]
H41 = [lambdify(Sym(h), (C₁₁, C₁₂, C₁₃, C₃₃, C₄₄, p¹...))(complex.(C_sev)..., p¹_num...) for h in eq41]
H_eq41 = TensTI{4}(real.(H41)..., (0.0, 0.0, 1.0))
H_lim(ω) = ω * inv(second_hill_tensor(Ellipsoid(1.0, 1.0, ω), C_sev_t))
n₃ = TensND.Tens([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
H_cod = 3 / 4 * sandwich(n₃, cod_tensor(PennyCrack(1.0), C_sev_t))
for ω in (1.0e-2, 1.0e-4, 1.0e-6)
    @printf "ω = %.0e   ω Q⁻¹ against eq. 41:  %.1e\n" ω relgap(H_lim(ω), H_eq41)
end

Where to go next ​

The coefficients derived here are those the theory page writes for the coaxial spheroid, and Spheroid in a transversely isotropic matrix shows how the package evaluates them without the losses met above. The flat limit is the starting point of the crack chapter: Crack opening displacement tensors derives the crack compliance for any anisotropy, of which eq. 41 is the transversely isotropic case. The tutorial Hill tensors by reduction to a sphere applies the reduction through the library on other shapes and matrices.
